label: rem:hecke-radical-is-temperley-lieb
title: The radical is the Temperley--Lieb ideal: $\sum \dim^{2}$ over the surviving blocks is $C_n$
html:
Convention D does not annihilate the three-strand antisymmetriser by accident. The row cap propagates up the whole tower, and what it leaves behind is a named algebra.

Because the fundamental representation of SU(2) is two-dimensional, no q-antisymmetriser exists on three of its strands, and the Wedderburn weight of any partition with three or more rows vanishes identically --- not numerically at q_0, but as a rational function of q. The surviving blocks of H_n(q) are therefore exactly the two-row shapes, which is the stratum the two-row stratum isolates for the {}^4\mathrm{He} fingerprint. Summing the squared Specht dimensions over those shapes gives, level by level, the Catalan numbers:

n surviving shapes \sum \dim^{2} \dim H_n(q) C_n
2 (2),\,(1,1) 2 2 2
3 (3),\,(2,1) 5 6 5
4 (4),\,(3,1),\,(2,2) 14 24 14
5 (5),\,(4,1),\,(3,2) 42 120 42
6 (6),\,(5,1),\,(4,2),\,(3,3) 132 720 132
7 (7),\,(6,1),\,(5,2),\,(4,3) 429 5040 429

The quotient of H_n(q) by the radical of its Markov form thus has the dimension of the Temperley--Lieb algebra TL_n(q), and the blocks match shape by shape. At n = 4 the bookkeeping closes exactly: 24 - 14 = 10 = 3^{2} + 1^{2}, the discarded (2,1,1) and (1^{4}) blocks, so the quotient is the direct sum of the three surviving matrix algebras and not a proper quotient of it.

Why the quotient is not an amputation

The metric obstruction below asks for a quotient by the radical, and taken on its own that reads as an ad hoc repair. It is not. The radical is the Temperley--Lieb ideal, generated by the three-strand q-antisymmetriser, and the quotient is a well-studied algebra with a diagrammatic calculus and a standard bilinear form. "Quotient by the radical" and "work in TL_n(q)" are one instruction.

Stated the other way: the degeneracy is not a defect convention D introduces, it is what convention D means. Under convention C the framework computes in the full Hecke algebra; under convention D it has been computing in Temperley--Lieb throughout.

What is measured and what is proved

The dimension count above was a measurement rather than a theorem of this paper; as of the Lean recorded below it is a theorem, at every n. The measurement came first and is kept, because it is what the theorem was checked against. The weights were evaluated for every partition of n = 2,\dots,7 at 50 decimal places, with worst residual 1.34 \times 10^{-51} against the closed form y_{(n-k,k)} = [n-2k+1]_q/[2]_q^{\,n}. That run is now recorded, and strengthened, in tl-two-row-weight-family.witness.json: rather than a residual at one q, the normalisation is checked as an exact identity in q,

  \sum_{k} f^{(n-k,k)}\,[n-2k+1]_q \;=\; [2]_q^{\,n},

which sympy simplifies to exactly 0 for n = 2,\dots,10 — so the closed form is a normalised weight family for every q at once, which no finite-precision evaluation can establish. The Specht dimensions are cross-checked by two independent routes (ballot and hook-length), and the table above is reproduced rather than cited.

What is now proved in Lean, at general n and sorry-free. Four statements, none of which is the isomorphism:

  • \sum_\lambda \dim_\lambda\, y_\lambda = 1 --- the normalisation \mathrm{tr}(1) = 1 (levelSum_eq_one);
  • \sum_k m_k(n)\,[n{+}1{-}2k]_q = [2]_q^{\,n} --- the same identity with the denominator cleared, i.e. the q-dimension count of V^{\otimes n} (qdim_normalisation_general);
  • \sum \dim^2 = C_n over the two-row shapes (dimHLF_two_row_sq_sum) and, separately, over the two-column shapes (dimHLF_two_col_sq_sum);
  • \dim \lambda = \dim \lambda' for this family (dimHLF_two_col_eq_two_row), which the next section had been asserting without backing.

What is still not proved: the isomorphism itself. No formalised statement of H_n(q)/\mathrm{rad} \cong TL_n(q) exists, and nothing above supplies one --- a count of blocks and a count of dimensions are not an isomorphism of algebras. The identification remains what this section calls it: something the counts support, deliberately not a proposition. What is available is the trace-theoretic half: the trace radical is a two-sided ideal (traceRadical_two_sided), which is what licenses passing to the quotient as an algebra at all, and convention D is the standard normalised Temperley--Lieb trace at loop parameter \delta = [2]_q (loop_reciprocal).

A convention collision to know about before wiring the Lean

QOU.MathlibExt.WenzlSchurElement proves the Temperley--Lieb stratification in the conjugate convention: at X = Q^{-N} the surviving blocks are those with \lambda_1 \le N, i.e. at most N columns. This section, and convention D, state the survivors as at most two rows. Both are correct in their own convention, and that file's own docstring warns: "anyone wiring schurElement_tl_eq_zero_iff to that block must transpose."

The trap is that the two conventions label different sets of partitions while carrying equal dimension sums. At n = 3 the row-set is \{(3),(2,1)\} and the column-set is \{(2,1),(1^3)\} — disjoint but for (2,1), both summing to 5; at n = 6 the two sets share nothing at all and both still total C_6 = 132. So the Catalan counts agree under either reading, and a check that looks only at dimensions cannot tell the two apart. Measured at n = 3,4,5 in tl-two-row-weight-family.witness.json.

Both halves of that trap are now theorems, at every n, in QOU.MassTheory.TwoRowTwoColumn: transposition is an explicit bijection between the two families (transposeEquiv), so they are equinumerous; the families are nevertheless different sets (atMostTwoRows_iff_atMostTwoCols_false, witnessed by the single row (3)); and their squared-dimension totals agree (dimHLF_two_col_sq_sum). The equality \dim \lambda = \dim \lambda' used above is proved there for this family (dimHLF_two_col_eq_two_row) rather than assumed --- it had been asserted here as though standard, and while it is standard for general partitions, nothing in this corpus had it.

The practical consequence: transposition is the only correct transport between the two conventions, and it is not the identity. Matching totals is not evidence that a theorem carries across.
